title: The Mysteries of Eleusis
bigQuestion: How did thousands of people keep one secret for more than a thousand years?

story.title: The Walk to Eleusis
story.kicker: A young woman from Athens joins thousands of walkers on a road that leads to a secret.
paragraphs: It is autumn in Athens, about 2,400 years ago. A young woman we will call Melissa stands in a huge crowd. Her mother stands beside her. Many people wear crowns of green leaves. Some carry long torches. Today they will walk the Sacred Way to a town called Eleusis.

The road is long, about 13 miles. The walkers sing. They call out the names of the gods. They pass farms and olive trees. Near the end, they see the blue sea. Melissa's feet hurt. But she keeps going. She has waited a long time for this day.

Night falls as the crowd reaches Eleusis. Torches light up a great stone hall. Melissa has made a promise. She will never tell what she sees inside. Thousands of people around her have made the same promise.

Later, Melissa walks home. She feels calm and full of hope. Friends ask her what happened inside the hall. She only smiles. Her secret is safe. Even today, historians do not know exactly what she saw. Melissa is a made-up person, but walks like hers really happened every year.
story.think: Why do you think Melissa kept her promise, even when her friends asked her what happened?

sections.title: A Holy Place and Its Story

lessons.title: A Holy Place Near Athens
lessons.mainIdea: Eleusis was a holy place near Athens where secret rites, called the Mysteries, were held for more than a thousand years.
reading: Eleusis is a town in Greece, about 13 miles west of the city of Athens. Long ago, Eleusis had a *sanctuary*. A sanctuary is a holy place with temples and altars. Strong walls kept it apart from the busy world outside.

Every year, people came to Eleusis for secret rites called the *Mysteries*. A rite is a set of holy actions done in a special order. Only people who had joined could see the most secret part. A person who joins through a special ceremony is called an *initiate*.

The Mysteries lasted more than a thousand years. Historians have strong evidence for them from the 500s BCE to the late 300s CE. Some think they began even earlier. Very few traditions in history have lasted that long.

words.d: a holy place with temples and altars, set apart from everyday life
the secret rites held at Eleusis, open only to people who had joined
a person who has joined a group through a special ceremony

look.title: A Map in Words
look.text: Picture a map of Greece. Find the big city of Athens near the sea. Now move your finger west, along the coast, about 13 miles. Stop at a small town beside a bay. That is Eleusis. A road runs between the two places. People called it the Sacred Way.
look.prompt: About how far was Eleusis from Athens? Name a place about that far from your school.

check.q: What is a sanctuary?
choices: A holy place with temples and altars
A long road between two towns
A secret word used by initiates
A crown made of green leaves
check.why: The reading says a sanctuary is a holy place with temples and altars.

check.q: About how long did the Mysteries of Eleusis last?
check.why: The reading says the Mysteries lasted more than a thousand years, from at least the 500s BCE to the late 300s CE.

check.q: What do we call a person who joins a group through a special ceremony?
check.why: An initiate is a person who has joined through a special ceremony.

lessons.title: Demeter Looks for Her Daughter
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone, who was taken to the land of the dead.
reading: The Greeks told a *myth* about two goddesses. A myth is an old story about gods or heroes. Demeter was the goddess of grain, the plants that give us bread. Her daughter was named Persephone. One day, Hades, king of the land of the dead, carried Persephone away.

Demeter searched everywhere for her daughter. She was so sad that she stopped helping plants grow. Fields turned brown. People had no grain to eat. At last, Zeus, the king of the gods, sent a messenger to bring Persephone back.

But Persephone had eaten a few pomegranate seeds in the land of the dead. So she had to go back for part of every year. When she returned to her mother, Demeter was happy and the fields grew green. Many people later read this as a story about the seasons.

words.d: an old story about gods or heroes that people told to explain the world
the Greek goddess of grain and harvest, honored at Eleusis
Demeter's daughter, who spent part of each year in the land of the dead

look.title: Fields in Two Seasons
look.text: Picture a field in two seasons. In one picture, the wheat is tall and gold. A woman carries a basket full of grain. In the other picture, the ground is brown and bare. Nothing grows. A cold wind blows over the empty field.
look.prompt: Which picture matches the time Persephone is with her mother? Explain how the myth fits the seasons.

check.q: What was Demeter the goddess of?
check.why: Demeter was the goddess of grain, the plants that give us bread.

check.q: What happened when Demeter was sad?
choices: Plants stopped growing and fields turned brown
check.why: In the myth, Demeter stopped helping plants grow, and the fields turned brown.

check.q: Why did Persephone have to go back to the land of the dead each year?
choices: She had eaten a few pomegranate seeds there
She wanted to rule the gods
She got lost on the Sacred Way
check.why: The myth says she ate pomegranate seeds in the land of the dead, so she had to return for part of every year.

lessons.title: The Hymn That Tells the Story
lessons.mainIdea: An old Greek poem, the Hymn to Demeter, tells the myth and says the goddess herself gave the rites to Eleusis.
reading: We know the myth from an old poem called the *Hymn to Demeter*. A *hymn* is a song or poem that praises a god. Nobody knows who wrote this one. Scholars think it was made about 2,600 years ago, around 600 BCE.

In the poem, sad Demeter wanders to Eleusis. She is dressed as an old woman, so no one knows her. The people of Eleusis are kind to her. Later, she tells them to build her a temple. There she teaches the leaders of the town her holy rites.

The hymn says the rites must not be told to others. It also says the people who have seen them are happy, or blessed. So the poem gives two big ideas at once: keep the secret, and the secret brings hope.

words.d: a song or poem that praises a god
an old Greek poem, from about 600 BCE, that tells the story of Demeter and Eleusis

look.title: What the Hymn Promises
look.text: Happy is the person on earth who has seen these rites. But the person who has not taken part will not have the same good share after death, down in the dark.
look.cite: Homeric Hymn to Demeter, about 600 BCE, near the end of the poem; retold from the translation by Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914
look.prompt: What does the hymn promise to people who have seen the rites? Why might that make someone want to join?

check.q: What is a hymn?
choices: A map of a holy place
A song or poem that praises a god
check.why: The reading explains that a hymn is a song or poem that praises a god.

check.q: How was Demeter dressed when she came to Eleusis in the poem?
check.why: In the Hymn to Demeter, she is dressed as an old woman, so no one knows her.

check.q: What two big ideas does the hymn give about the rites?
choices: Share them widely, and they bring money
Keep them secret, and they bring hope
Change them often, and they bring rain
Write them down, and they bring fame
check.why: The hymn says the rites must not be told, and it calls the people who saw them happy or blessed.

lessons.title: Who Could Join
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries were open to many kinds of people: men and women, rich and poor, free and enslaved, if they spoke Greek.
reading: Many Greek holy events were only for citizens of one city. Eleusis was different. Men and women could join. Rich and poor people could join. Even enslaved people could join. This made the Mysteries very unusual.
There were a few rules. A person had to understand Greek, so they could follow the words of the rites. A person who had killed someone could not join. Everyone else was welcome to begin.

Joining took steps. First, a person took part in smaller rites in the spring. Then, months later, they could come to the great rites in the autumn. Each new initiate had a guide who had already been through it. This guide was called a *mystagogue*.

words.d: a guide who had already joined and helped a new person through the Mysteries
forced to work for others without freedom or pay

look.title: Three People at the Gate
look.text: Three people stand at the gate. The first is a rich man from Athens. The second is a woman who sells bread in the market. The third is an enslaved worker from a farm. All three speak Greek. None of them has ever hurt anyone.
look.prompt: Using the rules in the reading, which of these three people could begin the Mysteries? Explain your answer.

check.q: What made the Mysteries of Eleusis unusual?
choices: Many kinds of people could join, even enslaved people
check.why: The reading says men, women, rich, poor and even enslaved people could join, which was unusual.

check.q: What did a person need to understand to join?
check.why: A person had to understand Greek to follow the words of the rites.

check.q: What was a mystagogue?
choices: A guide who helped a new initiate
check.why: A mystagogue was a guide who had already joined and helped a new person.

lessons.title: Walking the Sacred Way
lessons.mainIdea: In autumn, thousands of people walked about 13 miles from Athens to Eleusis in a great procession.
reading: The great rites came each autumn and lasted several days. First, the people gathered in Athens. They washed in the sea to make themselves clean for the goddess. Then came the most famous day: the long walk.

A *procession* is a large group walking together for a special reason. Thousands of people walked the road from Athens to Eleusis. This road was called the *Sacred Way*. It was about 13 miles long. Walkers carried torches, sang songs and called out to the gods.

The walk took most of the day. The crowd reached Eleusis as darkness fell. Walking together made strangers feel like one big group. Tired feet, shared songs and bright torches all became part of the memory.

words.d: a large group of people walking together for a special reason
the road, about 13 miles long, from Athens to Eleusis

look.title: The Road at Sunset
look.text: Picture the road at sunset. The sky is orange. Thousands of people fill the road. Some are old. Some are young. Torches glow in their hands. You can hear singing ahead and behind. Dust rises from the dry ground. Up ahead, walls and a great roof appear.
look.prompt: What would you hear, see and feel on this walk? How might walking together change how people felt about each other?

check.q: What is a procession?
choices: A large group walking together for a special reason
check.why: The reading defines a procession as a large group walking together for a special reason.

check.q: About how long was the Sacred Way?
check.why: The Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis was about 13 miles long.

check.q: When did the walkers reach Eleusis?
check.why: The reading says the crowd reached Eleusis as darkness fell.

lessons.title: Inside the Great Hall
lessons.mainIdea: The most secret part happened in a huge hall called the Telesterion, led by a high priest called the hierophant.
reading: At Eleusis stood a huge hall called the *Telesterion*. It was built so thousands of people could be inside at once. Rows of stone steps ran along the walls. In the middle was a small, special room.

The high priest was called the *hierophant*. The word means one who shows the holy things. On the most secret night, he showed the initiates something. People said there was bright light after darkness. But nobody wrote down exactly what was shown.

Initiates also drank a special drink made of barley and mint, called the kykeon. In the myth, Demeter drank it at Eleusis. Some modern writers have guessed that a mold from grain was in the drink and changed how people felt. Many historians doubt this, and no proof has been found.

words.d: the huge hall at Eleusis where the most secret rites took place
the high priest of Eleusis; the name means one who shows the holy things

look.title: What We Know and What We Do Not
look.text: What we know: the hall was huge. Thousands of people fit inside. A high priest showed holy things. Initiates drank a barley drink. What we do not know: exactly what was shown, what words were spoken, and what people saw in the light.
look.prompt: Why do you think the list of things we do not know is about the most secret part of the night?

check.q: What was the Telesterion?
choices: The huge hall where the secret rites took place
check.why: The Telesterion was the huge hall at Eleusis where the most secret rites happened.

check.q: What does the word hierophant mean?
choices: One who shows the holy things
check.why: The reading says hierophant means one who shows the holy things.

check.q: What do historians say about the idea that the kykeon had something in it that changed how people felt?
choices: Many doubt it, and no proof has been found
It was proved by a museum
check.why: The reading says many historians doubt this idea, and no proof has been found.

lessons.title: A Promise of Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Initiates promised to keep the rites secret, and in Athens telling or mocking them was a serious crime.
reading: Every initiate made a *vow* of silence. A vow is a serious promise. They could say that they had joined. They could say that it made them happy. But they could not tell what was shown or said inside the hall.

The city of Athens made this a law. Telling the secret, or making fun of the rites, was a serious crime. In 415 BCE, some rich young men were accused of acting out the Mysteries at private parties. The whole city was upset.

One man accused was Alcibiades, a famous general. He was away at war when Athens called him home for trial. He ran away to an enemy city instead. The story shows how much the people of Athens cared about the secret.

words.d: a serious promise, often made in a holy way
said to have done something wrong, before it is proven

look.title: What May I Say?
look.text: An initiate named Nikias comes home. His neighbor asks three questions. First: Did you go to Eleusis? Second: Did it make you feel good? Third: What did the priest show you in the hall?
look.prompt: Which questions could Nikias answer, and which one must he keep secret? Use the reading to explain.

check.q: What is a vow?
check.why: The reading says a vow is a serious promise.

check.q: What were some young men in Athens accused of in 415 BCE?
choices: Acting out the Mysteries at private parties
Walking the Sacred Way at night
check.why: In 415 BCE, some rich young men were accused of acting out the Mysteries at parties.

check.q: What did Alcibiades do when Athens called him home for trial?
choices: He ran away to an enemy city
check.why: The reading says Alcibiades ran away to an enemy city instead of facing trial.

lessons.title: What Old Writers Said
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient writers often mentioned the Mysteries but stopped before telling the secret; later enemies claimed to tell parts of it.
reading: Many writers in ancient times were initiates. They wrote that the Mysteries were beautiful and gave people hope. But when they came to the secret part, they stopped. Their silence is a kind of *evidence*, too. It shows how strong the promise was.

A travel writer named Pausanias visited Greece around 160 CE. He described many temples in detail. At Eleusis, he wrote that a dream warned him not to describe what was inside the walls. So he did not.

Around 200 CE, a Christian teacher named Clement of Alexandria wrote against the old religions. He claimed to tell some secret words of the rites. Historians use his words with care. He was an enemy of the rites, and enemies do not always report fairly.

words.d: facts or objects that help show what is true
a feeling for or against something that can change how a person tells about it

look.title: A Travel Writer Stops
look.text: My dream told me not to write about the things inside the wall of the sanctuary. And it is clear that people who have not joined may not learn about what they are not allowed to see.
look.cite: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Book 1, about 160 CE; retold from the translation by W. H. S. Jones, 1918
look.prompt: Pausanias describes many temples in detail. Why does he stop here? What does that tell you about the secret?

check.q: Why did Pausanias not describe what was inside the walls at Eleusis?
choices: He wrote that a dream warned him not to
He was not able to write
check.why: Pausanias wrote that a dream warned him not to describe what was inside the walls.

check.q: Why do historians use Clement of Alexandria's words with care?
choices: He was an enemy of the rites and may not report fairly
He lived in Eleusis all his life
He wrote in a secret code
check.why: Clement wrote against the old religions, and the reading says enemies do not always report fairly. That is bias.

check.q: How can a writer's silence be evidence?
choices: It proves the rites never happened
It shows how strong the promise of secrecy was
It shows the writer was an enemy
check.why: The reading says the writers' silence shows how strong the promise was.

lessons.title: A Picture From Ninnion
lessons.mainIdea: Objects like the Ninnion Tablet give us clues about the Mysteries, but even they do not show the final secret.
reading: Around 370 BCE, a woman named Ninnion gave a gift to the goddesses of Eleusis. It was a painted clay *tablet*, a flat board with a picture on it. People gave gifts like this to say thank you to the gods.

The tablet was buried for a very long time. Archaeologists found it at Eleusis in 1895. An *archaeologist* is a person who studies the past by digging up and looking at old things. Today the tablet is in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

The picture shows people walking with torches toward the goddesses. It is one of the rare pictures of the Mysteries that survive. It shows the way in. But it does not show the final secret. The picture keeps the secret, too.

words.d: a flat piece of clay, stone or wood with a picture or writing on it
a person who studies the past by digging up and looking at old things

look.title: Reading the Tablet
look.text: Picture a flat clay tablet, painted red and black. People walk in a line. Some hold torches. At one side, a goddess sits. The people are walking toward her. There are no words that tell what happens next.
look.prompt: What can you learn from this picture? What is still hidden?

check.q: Who gave the painted tablet to the goddesses?
check.why: The reading says a woman named Ninnion gave the tablet around 370 BCE.

check.q: What does an archaeologist do?
choices: Studies the past by digging up old things
check.why: An archaeologist studies the past by digging up and looking at old things.

check.q: What does the Ninnion Tablet NOT show?
choices: The final secret of the rites
check.why: The tablet shows the way in, but not the final secret.

sections.title: Why People Came, and the End

lessons.title: Hope and Belonging
lessons.mainIdea: People joined the Mysteries for hope about life after death and for the feeling of belonging to something great.
reading: Why would thousands of people walk 13 miles each year? One big reason was hope. The Greeks worried about what happens after death. The Hymn to Demeter said initiates would have a better share. Many people believed it.

Another reason was *belonging*. That is the feeling of being part of a group. At Eleusis, a farmer and a rich lord walked the same road. They kept the same secret. For a few days, they were all initiates together.
Later, even famous Romans came to join. The Roman speaker Cicero was an initiate. He wrote that the Mysteries helped people live well and face death with more hope. Some Roman emperors joined, too.

words.d: the feeling of being part of a group that accepts you
a life that some people believe comes after death

look.title: Two Reasons to Go
look.text: Two friends talk about going to Eleusis. Thea says, "I want to feel less afraid of what comes after this life." Dion says, "I want to walk with everyone, from farmers to lords, and be part of something big."
look.prompt: Which friend is talking about hope for the afterlife? Which one is talking about belonging? Which reason matters more to you?

check.q: What is belonging?
choices: The feeling of being part of a group
A promise to keep a secret
A long road to a temple
check.why: The reading defines belonging as the feeling of being part of a group.

check.q: What hope did the Hymn to Demeter give initiates?
choices: That they would never get sick
That they would win every war
That they would have a better share after death
check.why: The reading says the hymn promised initiates a better share after death.

check.q: Which famous Roman was an initiate at Eleusis?
check.why: The reading says the Roman speaker Cicero was an initiate.

lessons.title: The End of the Mysteries
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries ended in the late 300s CE, when Roman laws closed the old religions and the sanctuary was wrecked.
reading: By the 300s CE, Greece was part of the Roman Empire. Many people in the empire had become Christians. The emperors were Christian, too. They began to make laws against the old religions.

In 392 CE, Emperor Theodosius passed a law against the old rites. A few years later, in 396 CE, an army led by a man named Alaric wrecked the sanctuary at Eleusis. After more than a thousand years, the Mysteries came to an end. We call this kind of change a *decline*.

Today you can visit Eleusis. You can walk among the broken stones of the great hall. There is a small museum. But the secret went away with the last initiates. It is one of the best-kept secrets in history.

words.d: many lands and peoples ruled by one government or ruler
a slow change in which something gets weaker or smaller

look.title: How Long Ago?
look.cite: Dates from Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Princeton University Press, 1994, and the National Archaeological Museum, Athens
look.prompt: Which event happened longest ago? About how many years passed between the tablet being given and being found?

check.q: In what year did Emperor Theodosius pass a law against the old rites?
check.why: The reading says Theodosius passed the law in 392 CE.

check.q: What is an empire?
choices: A small town by the sea
Many lands and peoples ruled by one ruler
A song that praises a god
check.why: An empire is many lands and peoples ruled by one government or ruler, like the Roman Empire.

check.q: What happened to the secret of Eleusis when the rites ended?
choices: It went away with the last initiates
It was carved on the walls
It was printed in a book
It was painted on the Ninnion Tablet
check.why: The reading says the secret went away with the last initiates.

review.q: Which two goddesses were honored in the Mysteries of Eleusis?
review.why: The Mysteries honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone.

choices: The road from Athens to Eleusis
review.why: The Sacred Way was the road, about 13 miles long, that ran from Athens to Eleusis.

review.q: Who led the most secret part of the rites?
review.why: The hierophant, the high priest, showed the holy things in the Telesterion.

review.q: Which old poem tells the story of Demeter coming to Eleusis?
review.why: The Hymn to Demeter, from about 600 BCE, tells the myth and the start of the rites.

review.q: Which source is a painted clay picture found at Eleusis in 1895?
review.why: The Ninnion Tablet, given around 370 BCE, was found at Eleusis in 1895.

review.q: How are Pausanias and Clement of Alexandria different?
choices: Pausanias kept the secret; Clement, an enemy of the rites, claimed to tell parts of it
Pausanias was a priest; Clement was a king
Both told the whole secret clearly
Both were high priests at Eleusis
review.why: Pausanias stopped because of a dream; Clement wrote against the rites and claimed to reveal some words.

review.q: Which was NOT a rule for joining the Mysteries?
choices: You could not have killed someone
You had to be a rich man from Athens
You went through smaller rites first
review.why: Men and women, rich and poor, free and enslaved could join. Being rich was not a rule.

review.q: Why do historians still not know exactly what happened in the great hall?
choices: Initiates kept their vow of silence
review.why: Initiates promised silence, and the secret mostly held for more than a thousand years.
